name: SkinLens hybrid model
architecture: Image branch 1: EfficientNetV2-S (convolutional network, good at fine texture) - 1,280 features
Image branch 2: Swin Transformer V2-Base (vision transformer, good at overall shape) - 1,024 features
Patient-data branch: small neural network on age, sex and body site (21 inputs) - 32 features
Fusion: the 2,336 features are joined and passed to a classifier (512 units) that outputs 7 classes
Input image size 384 x 384 pixels; 108.3 million parameters

Prior correction: the model's probabilities are adjusted for how common each lesion type is (score = log p + 0.3 x log prior); the app shows these corrected probabilities. Settings: webapp/model_settings.json
Explanations: Grad-CAM (on the EfficientNetV2-S branch) and LIME
dataset: HAM10000 (Tschandl et al., Scientific Data 2018): 10,015 dermoscopic images of 7,470 lesions
7 classes: actinic keratosis, basal cell carcinoma, benign keratosis, dermatofibroma, melanoma, melanocytic nevus, vascular lesion
Lesion-grouped split: photos of the same lesion are never in both training and test (train 6,007 / validation 1,994 / test 2,014 images)
Very unbalanced: 67% of images are melanocytic nevi (moles); dermatofibroma and vascular lesions are rare
intended_use: A research and decision-support tool for doctors and trained staff looking at dermoscopic images of skin lesions.
It suggests the most likely lesion type, shows how confident it is, and explains where it looked.
The final decision always belongs to a qualified clinician (dermoscopy examination and, when needed, biopsy).
limitations: It does not make a diagnosis. It is not a certified medical device and has not been clinically validated.
It sometimes looks outside the lesion (e.g. at hair, rulers, ink marks or the image border); the heat-map shows when this happens, and such results deserve extra caution.
Limited data for darker skin tones: HAM10000 comes mostly from light-skinned patients (Fitzpatrick I-III), so performance on darker skin is unknown.

Rare classes have few training and test images (e.g. 22 dermatofibroma test images), so their results are less certain; about half of the 'melanoma' answers were false alarms in testing (precision 54% before prior correction).
Trained on dermoscopic images: ordinary phone photos may give unreliable results.
Numbers come from one test split of one dataset; results on images from other clinics may be lower.
summary_title: With prior correction (alpha = 0.3), as used by this app
summary_note: Without prior correction the original model had accuracy 85.45%, macro-F1 0.7603 (76.03%), melanoma recall 78.8% and ECE 0.159.
